summary: A summary listing of the RFCs in the 1500 to 1599 range. It serves as an index to that block of documents rather than specifying a protocol.

eli5.summary: A table of contents for a hundred notes. It tells you what each one is about.

subtitle: Annotated summary and index of RFC numbers 1500 through 1599.

tldr.problem: The RFC series grows continuously, and it is difficult for engineers to track what specifications exist in a particular range and understand their status and purpose.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a concise listing of all 100 RFCs numbered 1500 to 1599, with a one-sentence description of each and notation of which ones are on the standards track.
tldr.outcome: Engineers have a convenient reference showing what work has been standardized and what is experimental or informational during this period, marked clearly by purpose and status.

facts.label: Standards-track RFCs
facts.value: Majority of PPP, OSPF, MIME, SNMP, routing, security entries

today: RFC 1599 is Informational and serves as a historical reference. Published in January 1997, it documents the state of RFC work as of the mid-1990s. The RFCs it describes remain important: PPP is still used for dial-up and mobile connections; OSPF remains a widely deployed routing protocol; DHCP provides automatic IP configuration on most networks; MIME is foundational to email; and Kerberos is used in enterprise environments. The document is valuable for understanding what Internet engineers considered important and mature in the early 1990s, a period of significant growth and standardization.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content: RFC 1599 is an annotated index to RFC documents numbered 1500 through 1599. It provides a one-sentence description of each of the 100 RFCs in this range, helping readers quickly identify which RFCs might be relevant to their work. Entries that are on the IETF standards track are marked as [STANDARDS-TRACK]. The RFC notes that the status of standards-track RFCs may change during the standards process, and directs readers to the current 'Internet Official Protocol Standards' document for the definitive status of each specification. This document serves as a snapshot and historical record of the work published during the 1500 series.
sections.eli5: This note is a list. It has one-sentence summaries of 100 RFCs, from RFC 1500 to RFC 1599, and marks which ones are official standards.

sections.title: Content Overview by Category
sections.content: The RFCs in the 1500-1599 range cover a diverse set of topics reflecting the Internet's maturation in the early-to-mid 1990s. The collection includes core protocols and their extensions (PPP, OSPF, RIP, DNS, DHCP, IP multicast routing), management infrastructure (MIBs for SNMP, FDDI, Token Ring, DS1/E1, Frame Relay, SONET/SDH), security mechanisms (Kerberos, GSS-API), email and content standards (MIME, SMTP, X.400 gateways), directory services (LDAP, X.500, DNS), internationalization (character encodings for Japanese, Korean, Hebrew), and infrastructure services (remote printing, network monitoring, address allocation). Some are humor documents (April 1st RFCs), guidelines, tutorials, and meeting reports. The series captures Internet work transitioning from research to operational engineering, with growing attention to management, security, and heterogeneous network support.
sections.eli5: These 100 RFCs cover many topics: how to send data (PPP, OSPF), how to manage networks (MIBs, SNMP), how to keep data safe (Kerberos), how to send mail (MIME), and many other things the Internet needs.

sections.title: Standards Track and Experimental Protocols
sections.content: Many RFCs in the 1500-1599 range are on the standards track. Notably, the PPP protocol suite (RFCs 1548, 1549, 1570, 1572, 1598) defines the point-to-point protocol and its extensions for dial-up and leased-line links. The OSPF routing suite (RFCs 1583, 1584, 1587) specifies link-state routing. IP address allocation and aggregation (RFCs 1518, 1519, 1517) address the growing size of routing tables. The SNMP-based management infrastructure includes core MIBs for hosts (RFC 1514), interfaces (RFC 1573), FDDI (RFC 1512), token ring (RFC 1513), bridges (RFC 1525), and various protocol-specific MIBs. DHCP (RFC 1541) and BOOTP (RFC 1542, 1532) provide automatic host configuration. Security standards include Kerberos V5 (RFC 1510), GSS-API (RFC 1508, 1509), and authentication frameworks (RFC 1511). MIME standards (RFCs 1521, 1522) establish how non-ASCII content is transmitted in email. Other track entries cover routing extensions, ATM/IP interaction, and protocol clarifications.
sections.eli5: Many of these RFCs are official standards. They include PPP (for dial-up), OSPF (for routing), DHCP (to give computers IP addresses), Kerberos (for security), and MIME (for email with pictures and formatting).

sections.title: Informational and Experimental RFCs
sections.content: A significant portion of the 1500-1599 range consists of informational RFCs. These include engineering notes and guidelines (RFC 1586: OSPF over Frame Relay; RFC 1580: Network Resource Tools), tutorials and meeting reports (RFC 1506: X.400 gateway tutorial; RFC 1588: White Pages meeting report), FYI documents answering frequently asked questions (RFC 1594: New Internet user questions; RFC 1578: Primary and secondary school user questions), analyses and experience reports (RFC 1585: MOSPF analysis; RFC 1581: RIP extensions analysis), character encoding and internationalization standards (RFCs 1554, 1555, 1556, 1557, 1563), and protocol specifications for specialized uses (RFC 1569: Radio paging; RFC 1528, 1529, 1530: Remote printing via email). The experimental category includes work on TUBA/CLNP transition (RFC 1561), extension mechanisms for protocols (RFC 1505: Encoding header), and novel applications of existing infrastructure. These documents provide implementation guidance, capture operational experience, and explore future directions without requiring standards-track consensus.
sections.eli5: Some of these are just notes and guidelines, not official standards. They share examples of how to use protocols, lessons learned, and answers to common questions. Some are experiments with new ideas.

sections.title: Status and Significance
sections.content: RFC 1599 itself is marked Informational; it does not define or update any protocol. It is a historical snapshot of Internet standardization as of early 1997, covering RFCs published mostly between 1993 and 1994. The document is valuable as a reference point showing what was considered important and ready for standardization in that era: Internet infrastructure (routing, addressing, DNS), network management (SNMP MIBs), security basics (Kerberos), and foundational email standards (MIME). Notably absent from this range are major application-layer protocols (those came earlier and later) and the World Wide Web (which was also developing in parallel). The summary reflects a period of transition, with TCP/IP becoming the dominant network model, IPv4 address exhaustion beginning to be a concern, and the Internet moving from experimental to operational. Each RFC listed here contributes to understanding the state of Internet protocols at that point in time.
sections.eli5: This note is just a list and summary, not a standard itself. It shows what the Internet community thought was important in 1994. It is useful for understanding what protocols were being made official standards back then.
